statements.status_notes: sha256crypt and sha512crypt through 0.6 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) because the algorithm's runtime is proportional to the square of the length of the password.
statements.impact_statement: glibc sha256crypt/sha512crypt algorithmic-complexity denial-of-service issue (CPU cost proportional to the square of password length), which Ubuntu has marked Ignored as architectural (will never be fixed without migrating hash schemes). Affects crypt(3) password hashing, which the JVM never calls.

statements.status_notes: Passing an effectively empty string to the ",ccs=" syntax extension of the mode argument in the fopen function in the GNU C Library version 2.45 or earlier may result in a heap buffer overflow when the mode string input to the function is attacker controlled. This usage pattern is not seen in applications in common GNU/Linux distributions.
statements.impact_statement: This heap buffer overflow requires an application to call glibc's fopen function with an attacker-controlled mode string containing an effectively empty ",ccs=" syntax extension. Liquibase Secure's runtime never constructs fopen mode strings from external input; the JVM's own file I/O does not use this glibc idiom.

statements.status_notes: Calling strfmon and strfmon_l in the GNU C Library version 2.38 to 2.44 can write past the end of the caller-supplied output buffer when a conversion uses right-justified width padding. At the time of publication, no network-facing application impact is known.
statements.impact_statement: This glibc flaw is reachable only through application calls to strfmon or strfmon_l with a vulnerable right-justified width-padding pattern. The Liquibase Secure image inherits the OS package from eclipse-temurin:21-jre-noble (`docker/Dockerfile:2`) and the container entrypoint execs only the Liquibase CLI (`docker/docker-entrypoint.sh:8`, `docker/docker-entrypoint.sh:119`). A focused grep across the runtime Dockerfiles, entrypoint scripts, and application source found no references to strfmon or strfmon_l, so the vulnerable API path is not reachable from the stock Liquibase Secure runtime.

statements.status_notes: Calling tdelete on a sufficiently deep tree in the GNU C Library version 2.1 to 2.44 may write one pointer past the end of an alloca-allocated array on the stack, which may crash the application. No affected application in common distributions has been identified.
statements.impact_statement: This glibc flaw requires an application to use tsearch/tdelete on a very deep tree. The Liquibase Secure image inherits the OS package from eclipse-temurin:21-jre-noble (`docker/Dockerfile:2`) and the container entrypoint execs only the Liquibase CLI (`docker/docker-entrypoint.sh:8`, `docker/docker-entrypoint.sh:119`). A focused grep across the runtime Dockerfiles, entrypoint scripts, and application source found no references to tsearch or tdelete, so the vulnerable API path is not reachable from the stock Liquibase Secure runtime.

statements.status_notes: The iconv() function in the GNU C Library versions 2.43 and earlier may crash due to an assertion failure when converting inputs from the IBM1390 or IBM1399 character sets, which may be used to remotely crash an application. This vulnerability can be trivially mitigated by removing the IBM1390 and IBM1399 character sets from systems that do not need them.
statements.impact_statement: The scanned image reports libc-bin 2.39-0ubuntu8.7, below Ubuntu's fixed 2.39-0ubuntu8.8, but this issue requires an application to process IBM1390 or IBM1399 encoded input through glibc's iconv conversion path. The stock Liquibase Secure runtime is the Liquibase Java CLI, and a review of its build and runtime path found no references to iconv or those IBM1390 or IBM1399 code pages.

statements.status_notes: The deprecated functions ns_printrrf, ns_printrr and fp_nquery in the GNU C Library version 2.2 and newer fail to enforce the caller-supplied buffer length, and can result in an out-of-bounds write when printing TSIG records.
statements.impact_statement: This CVE affects deprecated glibc resolver-printing functions used for TSIG record formatting. Liquibase Secure's stock runtime is the Liquibase Java CLI, and a source review found no references to ns_printrrf, ns_printrr, fp_nquery, or TSIG processing in the product runtime path. libc-bin is inherited from the base image only, so the vulnerable glibc function path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: Calling wordexp with WRDE_APPEND in the GNU C Library version 2.0 to version 2.43 can cause the interface to return invalid memory in the we_wordv member, which on subsequent calls to wordfree may abort the process.
statements.impact_statement: This flaw requires an application to call glibc's wordexp function with the WRDE_APPEND flag. Neither the JVM nor the container's bash entrypoint calls wordexp; this is a C-language shell-word-expansion API that Liquibase Secure's Java and bash-only runtime path never invokes.

statements.status_notes: When expanding paths that begin with a tilde followed by a username, glibc's parse_tilde allocates the extracted username on the stack with strndupa based on untrusted input length. If an application passes attacker-controlled input to wordexp, an excessively long username can exhaust stack space and trigger a stack clash.
statements.impact_statement: The scanned image reports libc-bin 2.35-0ubuntu3.10, below Ubuntu's fixed 2.35-0ubuntu3.15, but this flaw requires an application to pass attacker-controlled input into glibc's wordexp path-expansion API. The stock Liquibase Secure runtime is the Liquibase Java CLI behind a bash-based entrypoint, and a source review found no references to wordexp or WRDE_APPEND in the container build or runtime path.

statements.status_notes: Converting crafted SHIFT_JISX0213 input to UCS-4 or the internal wide character encoding, for example with iconv, in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to 2.44 may result in the converter making no progress, causing the calling application to hang.
statements.impact_statement: The scanned image reports libc-bin 2.35-0ubuntu3.10, below Ubuntu's fixed 2.35-0ubuntu3.15, but this issue requires an application to feed attacker-controlled SHIFT_JISX0213 data through glibc's iconv conversion path with a small enough output buffer to split a two-code-point decode. Liquibase Secure's stock runtime path is the Java CLI, and a review of its build and runtime flow found no references to iconv or SHIFT_JISX0213 processing. The vulnerable glibc conversion path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: Converting crafted EUC_JISX0213 input to UCS-4 or the internal wide character encoding, for example with iconv, in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to 2.44 may result in the converter making no progress, causing the calling application to hang.
statements.impact_statement: The scanned image reports libc-bin 2.35-0ubuntu3.10, below Ubuntu's fixed 2.35-0ubuntu3.15, but this issue requires an application to feed attacker-controlled EUC_JISX0213 data through glibc's iconv conversion path with a small enough output buffer to split a two-code-point decode. Liquibase Secure's stock runtime path is the Java CLI, and a review of its build and runtime flow found no references to iconv or EUC_JISX0213 processing. The vulnerable glibc conversion path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: Initializing the DNS stub resolver from an /etc/resolv.conf file, or a LOCALDOMAIN environment variable, whose search list contains a domain of roughly 200 characters or more in the GNU C Library version 2.26 to 2.44 results in an assertion failure which aborts the process. The resolver truncates the search list when copying it into the fixed-size _res.defdname buffer, then asserts that the copy is consistent with the full configuration. The consistency check compared against the wrong size and did not handle a first entry that does not fit, so a correctly truncated list failed the assertion. Any process that resolves names through the library is affected, including long-running processes that reload /etc/resolv.conf on the next query after it changes. Search domains are commonly written to /etc/resolv.conf from data received over DHCP or from a VPN server, so an attacker on the local network may be able to trigger this without privileges on the target system, subject to validation by the network configuration software.
statements.impact_statement: glibc DNS stub resolver assertion-abort issue when /etc/resolv.conf or LOCALDOMAIN contains a ~200+ character search-list domain. Requires attacker control of the container's DNS configuration; not remotely triggerable against this image.

statements.status_notes: The nscd service in the GNU C Library 2.3.4 onwards may crash due to a stack overflow when a malicious DNS server returns too large a response for a DNS query, resulting in degraded DNS resolution for the system. Exploitation of this bug needs a system that has nscd enabled and using an untrusted DNS server for name resolution, with the compromised DNS server being capable of processing records large enough to result in a stack overflow in an nscd thread stack. During experimentation, bind 9 was unable to handle large records, but that could change in future or with a different name server. In typical installations, nscd is executed in an isolated context as its own user without a shell, due to which any compromise of that service is isolated. There is a remote possibility of nscd cache corruption if an attacker manages to get the stack pointer into a desired point in the heap, potentially resulting in other caches in nscd being overwritten with corrupt data through the stack overflow, until the buggy code path eventually results in a crash. Finally, a crash in nscd may result in performance degradation when resolving names, but it does not result in a denial of service.
statements.impact_statement: glibc nscd stack-overflow crash when a malicious DNS server returns an oversized response. Requires nscd running against an untrusted DNS server; this minimal image runs no nscd process at all.
